World.title: Orissa HC orders probe into police ‘excesses’ on tribal villagers resisting bauxite mining
World.content: B The Orissa High Court has directed Rayagada district administration to submit a report in connection with alleged police excesses on tribal villagers opposed to a bauxite mining project near their village. Hearing a public interest litigation filed by Purushottam Hikaka and seven others, a Division Bench of Chief Justice Harish Tandon and Justice Chittaranjan Dash directed the administration to maintain peace in villages close to mining site in Sijimali Hill located in the Rayagada and Kalahandi districts. Several villagers have opposed the mining proposal saying it would destroy the surrounding water sources, ecology and their livelihood. The resistance intensified after Rayagada district administration tried to facilitate the laying of a road to mining site. The April 7 order was made available online on Thursday. The petitioners alleged that police personnel raided homes in the early hours of March 10 in Kalahandi district, ransacked houses and arrested 21 villagers, including 10 women. It was also alleged that several cases were lodged against the villagers under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 and they were put into Bhawanipatna jail. “The random house raids by breaking the doors were done by the police personnel which is violative of the guidelines laid down in the case of D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal,” argued advocate Anup Kumar Mohapatra, counsel for petitioners. The petitioners also narrated inhumane treatment of a 19-year-old pregnant woman and three other women and their children. These women were arrested without communicating the reason for their detention. State counsel Saswat Das submitted that the police had gone to execute non-bailable warrants issued by the court but in the course of discharging their duties, they were attacked, resulting in injuries to 58 police personnel. The matter will come up next on September 2.

World.title: Bengaluru to host India International Coffee Festival in February 2027
World.content:
India’s coffee industry is gearing up for its next phase of growth as the India International Coffee Festival (IICF) returns to Bengaluru from February 26 to 28, 2027.

Organised by the Coffee Board of India in association with the Specialty Coffee Association of India (SCAI), the third edition of IICF will bring together growers, roasters, café brands, baristas, equipment manufacturers, and coffee consumers on a farm-to-cup platform.

The event comes as domestic coffee consumption shows significant room for expansion. While cities account for nearly 70% of consumption and southern India contributes 75-80% of the country’s coffee consumption, coffee is gaining popularity in northern, western and eastern markets. India’s per-capita coffee consumption remains at just 0.07 kg annually, compared with the global average of 1.3 kg.

“IICF has become an important platform for India’s coffee community at a time of remarkable growth,” said Kurma Rao M., CEO & Secretary, Coffee Board of India. “As café culture spreads across India and a new generation embraces coffee, the home market holds enormous potential, even as Indian coffee earns its place on the world stage.”

“India has grown some of the finest coffee on Earth for generations, and now, at last, India is drinking it,” said Hamsini Appadurai, President, SCAI and organiser, IICF.

A key attraction at the conference will be the National Coffee Championships, including the 26th National Barista Championship, Brewers Cup, Indian Filter Coffee Championship, Latte Art Championship, and, for the first time, Coffee in Good Spirits. Winners will represent India at corresponding World Coffee Championships.

The championship qualifiers will be held in Bengaluru, Delhi and Navi Mumbai between August and October 2026, ahead of the national finals in Bengaluru.

World.title: Roastery Coffee House opens a Taramati Baradari-inspired café in Hyderabad
World.content:
Taramati Baradari is a historic open-air pavilion built during the Qutb Shahi era, known for its striking architecture. Roastery Coffee House's latest outlet in Film Nagar — its third in Hyderabad and 15th nationally — is a contemporary interpretation of the 17th-century dance pavilion.

Founder Nishant Sinha says the café borrows the original structure's strong geometry, repeated arches, symmetry and rhythm. Natural light streams through the arches, adding warmth to the space. Unlike the monochromatic original, however, the café gets a playful update with pink, yellow, mint green and blue across its walls. The result is a colourful take on Hyderabad's architectural heritage.

The Moorish-style pointed arches and balustrade railing are among the first details to catch the eye. The patterns create a sense of order and repetition, offering a contemporary take on the ornamental geometry found in historic Deccan architecture.

“We added colour because we wanted the space to feel happy and translate that feeling into the café environment,” says Nishant.

The café also brings in a distinctly Telugu touch through its upholstery. Custom-printed Kalamkari fabric adds colour to the otherwise pared-back interiors. “We have kept the interiors simple to keep the focus on the coffee bar. The centrepiece is a customised Kalamkari artwork featuring Indian coffee beans. We have copyrighted the piece as well,” says Nishant.

The café’s outdoor area draws from the open-air gardens of Taramati Baradari. The only dampener is the presence of flies, an increasingly common nuisance in Hyderabad.

The food menu sticks to familiar café fare, without unnecessary desi twists on Asian dishes. Sandwiches, pasta and finger foods are among the popular picks.

The club sandwich remains my personal favourite, though the hold-in sandwich, with chicken and avocado, is giving it some competition.

What does one drink here? There is no shortage of coffee. The cappuccino is a bestseller among the hot beverages, while my pick is the Monsoon Malabar hot pour-over, made with a microlot bean. The café's Gungegiri Estate beans recently won a Gold Award at the Global Coffee Awards (Asia), held in Charleston, US.

Among the cold drinks, the trademarked cranberry coffee is the bestseller. Crisp and tart, it combines cranberry with coffee for a refreshing drink. I prefer the lychee coffee, though, simply because I love lychee. Other popular cold options include the brownie blend coffee and the cold coffee, available with or without ice cream.

The café is cheerful and relaxed, but the high ceiling makes the acoustics a little challenging — a problem the management is working on. This isn’t a place for whispered sweet nothings. It's the kind of café where you can talk loudly, eat with your hands and slurp your cold coffee without worrying about anyone judging you. Most milk-based coffees can also be customised with vegan milk.

What's next, I ask Nishant? "Bengaluru, with another exciting design to talk about."

All Roastery Coffee House outlets are open from 8am utill 11 pm.

World.title: How Mudapuram in Thiruvananthapuram is attracting visitors this Onam
World.content:
A rain-kissed morning was the perfect premise to set foot at Mudapuram. Scores of Reels and shorts on social media were reason enough to land up at this sleepy village near Chirayinkeezhu, located about 30 kilometres from Thiruvananthapuram city. People have been flocking here to watch and click photos at the tree house, named Mudapurathe Onakkudil (Onam hut of Mudapuram), erected at the centre of the paddy field that stretches as far as eyes could see. To complement the setting, there are marigold plants with yellow and orange blooms grown on two sides of the canal that runs through the field.

The tree house has a backstory to it, says Ajeesh Ramdas, president of Mudapuram Residents’ Association (MUDRA), which maintains the structure. “Last year, a month before Onam, a group of youngsters from here had put up a hut made of bamboo and thatched with palm leaves in the middle of the field. They had planned it as a setting to take photographs during Onam. But the same night it was destroyed by someone. Anti-social elements had been causing troubles for quite sometime and that incident was the last straw. So we decided to revive the then-defunct residents’ association and construct a permanent structure,” says Ajeesh, who runs a construction company, Iron Mode.

His company sponsored the construction of a permanent structure with metal frame and tiled roof. “We opened it on Atham (first day of 10-day Onam festival) day last year itself. Social media gave us a lot of traction. This year, we have gone a step ahead and planted marigold plants to attract more people,” says Sumesh MS, joint secretary of MUDRA.

Subin S, secretary of MUDRA, who led the effort to plant marigolds on a half kilometre stretch using mulching sheets, says, “We got around 3000 saplings via Kudumbashree and the planting started in June. Since we residents were finding it difficult to do it alone, we sought the help of women who work under Viksit Bharat – Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission. But the real challenge was when we lost a lot of plants because of a pest attack, which we are still fighting.”

Meanwhile, on the paddy field, covering around eight acres, farming is carried out by different people, who have formed a collective called Thengumvila Padasekhara Samithi, comprising 30-plus members. “The field was lying unused for quite some time. A few of us came together, took it on lease from the owners and started cultivation. The harvest was so good that the owners themselves evinced interest to take up farming the following year,” Ajeesh says.

However, the paddy plants you see now were not planted by the Samithi. “They have come up from the grains that fell off the stalks during harvest,” Sumesh says.

Thengumvila Bhagavathy Temple, located close to the field, also cultivates paddy on a few cents. As has been the practice, the Temple gets to harvest the produce first. Also, during Onam, the first swing in the region is put up at the temple.

MUDRA office-bearers unanimously say that there has been tremendous support and encouragement from several quarters to put Mudapuram on tourism map. Eight park benches installed by the roadside close to the field have been sponsored by eight people. Ajeesh adds, “We have been planning to install CCTV cameras and when I put forward the budget required, we collected the amount within a couple of days.”

Among those who support the initiative are Thengumvila Temple Trust, SNDP Yogam, Government UP School, Thengumvila Padasekhara Samithi and the residents from in and around Mudapuram who work or live abroad. Kizhuvalam panchayat and agriculture office have also extended helping hand, they say.

Plans are in place to start flower cultivation on permanent basis. The residents are also exploring the possibility of removing the wild growth and cleaning the deep chira (bund) at one end of the field and launch a country boat. “We hope to bring in more development and increase tourist footfall by next year,” the office bearers say.

How to reach: Follow Google Map by typing Mudapuram Onakkudil.

World.title: Madras Day 2026: the humble typewriter keeps clacking despite the digital takeover
World.content:
A chorus of clickety-clacks from manual typewriters drowns the bustle on Jaganathapuram First Street, which sits in a tract of Chetpet where every house leans into the next somewhat like books in a library shelf. Inside, as young fingers dance over ageing manual typewriters , kept sprightly by consistent maintenance, teacher-plus-owner of Chetpet Typewriting Institute (est. 1975) P. Padmanabhan is supervising yet another class, spelling out instructions to students.

Typing proficiency, whioh includes speed, opening doors to certain clerical positions in government and private settings, being an essential component in certain competitive government exams including TNPSC Group IV, some categories of Staff Selection Commission, institutes of this nature still thrive. Padmanabhan points out every class includes students who view the acquisition of typing skill as an end in itself; just being able to type fast and error-free is good enough. Therefore, also expect those training for careers in law, the corporate world and so on to walk in through those doors, says Padmanabhan, adding that he receives students from near and far and the institute's current strength is 50.

A plea to the Tamil Nadu Government Typewriting institutes are anxious over a government order dated October 28, 2024 stating that the Directorate of Technical Education (DoTE) in Tamil Nadu would be doing away with the practice of having typing exams on manual typewriters, shifting them to computers from February 2028. Echoing the collective sentiment of associations representing typewriting institutes across the state, J. Srinivasan of Karumari Technical Institute in Saidapet, told The Hindu Downtown that typewriting exams in English and Tamil should be conducted only on typewriters. He points out, “Besides, the Computer on Office Automation (COA) exam should not be merged with the English and Tamil typewriting exams. Instead, the current system of conducing the three exams separately with a separate certificate given for each should continue. Every year, more than one lakh students take typing exams, conducted every six months. Clubbing them with COA will reduce the number of takers; and that will result in reduced revenue for the government.” Srinivasan adds that switching typing exams from manual typewriters to computers will affect the livelihoods of typewriting institutes and typewriter mechanics across Tamil Nadu, which he estimates at around 5000 and 2000 respectively. He states: “Associations and federations representing these institutes and mechanics want this GO cancelled.”

And these multiple needs keep these instruments going, refurbished from time to time. Chetpet Typewriting Institute is not the oldest, but is symbolic of typewriting institutes, continuing with unflagging enthusiasm despite challenges from technology.

Padmanabhan belabours manual typewriter-based institutes’ continuing relevance, citing numbers and benefits. “There are 4,500 government-approved typewriting institutes across Tamil Nadu,” he states. “Typewriting equips a person to type faster and more efficiently. Once you master it, operating a computer becomes effortless.”

This belief has had Padmanabhan, now aged 75, wearing a new hat post his retirement as medical photo officer (also known as ‘medical photographer’) from Rajiv Gandhi Government Hospital in 2006, taking the mantle from his father and running Chetpet Typewriting Institute. The institute operating from a space, quite an expansive space, in Padmanabhan’s house, makes the overheads of running it manageable. Without a soupcon of regret, he points out he whittled down the number of institutes he ran from seven to one. “Unable to find teachers of the calibre I sought, I shut down the institutes.”

He notes with quiet pride, “I am a certified high-speed typewriting expert and an official government examiner,” recognised by the Tamil Nadu Directorate of Technical Education (DOTE). Padmanabhan personally teaches both Tamil and English typewriting; shorthand classes are also offered. His voice resonating with justifiable pride, he says: “Search my name online, you will find it.”

Decades ago, every street probably sported a typewriting institute. Those like Padmanabhan maintain their numbers would have dwindled but not their relevance. And this is why, 20 years after retirement, he continues to fill his house with a chorus of clickety-clacks.

A typewriter mechanic on wheels

The phone rings, and within minutes, 54-year-old S. Thyagarajan is on his way to ‘rescue’ another manual typewriter. There is no workshop, no colourful signboards announcing his trade. He is the workshop on the move; and his experience repairing manual typewriters since 1986 is the signboard. Owners of typewriting institutes across Chennai have his number saved as “ICE”. That is obviously hyperbole, but typewriter mechanics such as Thyagarajan are indeed indispensable in “emergency” situations involving these machines, as brands selling manual typewriters have long ceased production, and the old machines have to be kept in circulation.

Thyagarajan entered the profession in 1986 soon after completing Class 10, having been born into a family of typewriter mechanics, his grandfather and uncle particularly known in the trade. The clatter of these machines defines his earliest memories, and he is among a dedicated group of people who refuse to let manual typewriters become a memory.

While typewriter manufacturers have ceased production, he says, typewriters are far from extinction. “The spare parts still come from Delhi. A manufacturer who started the business when typewriters were in their heyday continues to supply them even today,” he explains.

He notes that around 40 regular customers, including several typewriting institutes continue to rely on his services. Thyagarajan once ran repair shops which he shut down as rents escalated. Today, he follows what can be called a more practical approach.

“ Every occupation evolves with time. One phone is enough to run the business now. Maintaining shops has become an unnecessary expense,” he says.

He is a a staunch believer not only in these machines, but also what they bring to the table, well sheet. He is emphatic that those trained on typewriters make fewer mistakes because their fingers develop greater speed and accuracy, whereas those who learn typing directly on computer keyboards are more error-prone, particularly while typing Indian languages such as Tamil.

“Even my name has been misspelt umpteen number of times,” he remarks bitterly, adding that such mistakes can create unnecessary complications in government records and other important documents.

And for that reason and also for the fact that livelihoods still depend on typewriting institutes, he wants these old machines to continue clicking away in classrooms and examination halls.

(Ahead of Madras Day, Resilience Series tracks institutions and industries that had their heyday when the city was Madras are up against difficult times now, but are soldiering on with inimitable poise.)

World.title: Entries invited for Love of Advertising Awards instituted by Advertising Club Trivandrum
World.content:
Advertising Club Trivandrum (ACT), the community of  and media professionals in Thiruvananthapuram, has invited entries for the inaugural Love of Advertising (LoA) awards. It will celebrate and reward excellence in advertising, media, design, digital communication and brand building from across India.

A statement issued by ACT says that awards will be given in a dozen categories. Works released between January 1, 2025, and March 31, 2026, are eligible to enter the competition. Those involved in the creation of a campaign can submit the entry, provided they meet the criteria. This includes advertising agencies, media organisations, clients, client partners, production houses, design studios, digital partners or individuals, as specified under each category.

Content creators and influencers can submit their entries in Creator-led Branded Content category. Agencies, individuals and students can submit entries in unpublished work categories. In addition, there is an Independent Creative Excellence category, which is for non-branded work from freelancers, in-house designers and studios.

The statement mentions that the 10-member jury has some of the eminent names from the industry and is headed by veteran Bobby Pawar, former chairman and chief creative officer at Havas Group. Laj Salam, president of ACT, says in a statement, “Through the awards we want to celebrate not just great campaigns, but the passion, craft and commitment behind them. Our vision is to build an awards platform that earns national respect while inspiring the next generation of creative professionals.” Vishnu Vijay, secretary of ACT, adds, “ACT was formed to create a vibrant community where professionals can learn, collaborate and grow together. The LoA Awards is a natural extension of that vision.”

Formed in February 2025 as a non-profit body bringing together advertising, media and communication professionals from Thiruvananthapuram, ACT currently has over 100 members. Filmmaker and advertising veteran R Balki officially inaugurated the club in March 2025 and actor Mohanlal released the logo.

ACT has carried out several initiatives since its formation, including interactive sessions, networking events, student outreach programmes, sports-based programmes and industry visits, the statement says. Notable among them has been a session to commemorate advertising legend Piyush Pandey by Sneha Iype, founder-partner and executive producer, Nirvana Films, and a knowledge session led by first Cannes Lion award winner and an industry veteran Senthil Kumar. ACT marked its first anniversary with an interactive session between Member of Parliament and author Shashi Tharoor and LV Navaneeth, CEO of The Hindu Group.

According to the office-bearers, through LoA, the Club has joined the league of prominent advertising clubs across the country that have been recognising creative excellence on a grand scale.

Last date for receiving entries is August 31. Details on www.loaawards.com
